section_title: How does knowing God shape the way we live?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 9 For this reason, since the day we heard about you, we have not stopped praying for you and asking God to fill you with the knowledge of His will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding, 10 so that you may walk in a manner worthy of the Lord and may please Him in every way: bearing fruit in every good work, growing in the knowledge of God, 11 being strengthened with all power according to His glorious might so that you may have full endurance and patience, and joyfully

12 giving thanks to the Father, who has qualified you to share in the inheritance of the saints in the light. 13 He has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of His beloved Son, 14 in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.

context_lines: The report of the Colossians’ faith and love moves Paul from thanksgiving into a continuing prayer for them. He asks God to fill them with the knowledge of His will, with spiritual wisdom and understanding.

The purpose of that knowledge is a life pleasing to the Lord. Paul describes good works, growing knowledge of God, endurance and patience. Knowing and living belong together: the prayer reaches into what they do and how they persevere.

The power he asks for is God’s power. Its stated purpose here includes patient endurance. Paul does not equate strength with escaping every difficulty; he asks for what will sustain a faithful life through it.

The prayer leads into thanksgiving to the Father, who has qualified them to share in the saints’ inheritance in the light. He has rescued them from darkness and brought them into His beloved Son’s kingdom. Their life of growth rests on His saving action.

In the Son they have redemption, explained here as the forgiveness of sins. The passage moves from prayer for a worthy life to the reason for grateful confidence: God has acted to bring them to Himself through Christ.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly read this as prayer for knowledge that bears fruit in a changed life. [Wesley’s notes on verses 9–11](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-colossians/) connect understanding God’s will with conduct and patient endurance. The [USCCB note on verses 9–14](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/colossians/1) also describes the interaction between knowing God and living according to the gospel. This is an active life of dependence on Him.
The closing verses are commonly read as thanksgiving for God’s rescue and forgiveness through His Son. They supply the basis for the growing life Paul asks God to sustain.
god_plan_lines: In [Acts 26:15–18](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/26.htm), the risen Jesus sends Paul to the Gentiles so they may turn from darkness to light, receive forgiveness and share an inheritance among those sanctified by faith in Him. The same connected themes appear here in a community that has received the gospel.

This rescue reaches beyond an individual improvement project. God is bringing people into His Son’s kingdom and forming their lives in keeping with that belonging. Paul’s stated aim in [Colossians 1:27–29](https://biblehub.com/bsb/colossians/1.htm) is to present people mature in Christ, with the hope of glory. The prayer and the thanksgiving belong to that one work.
current_position_lines: In [What Does Prayer Look Like?](https://thewayofscripture.com/studies/what-does-prayer-look-like.html), we draw attention to what Paul asks for here: deeper knowledge of God’s will, a life that honors Him, good fruit and strength to endure. This passage gives us a positive pattern for praying for another person’s growth in Christ.

editorial_review.position_source_detail: What Does Prayer Look Like?, Colossians 1:9–11 and surrounding comparison, lines 116–126. Positive prayer for knowledge, conduct and endurance only; no blanket claim that Paul never asks for a changed circumstance.
